items.prose: A model predicts each share's return over days 1 to 21 at the close of day 0. One feature is the size of the earnings surprise in the next quarterly report. For most shares that report lands around day 15.
items.question: Can the feature be used?

options.text: No: for most shares it is known only on about day 15
Yes: earnings are fundamental data, not prices
options.why: The kind of data does not matter. What matters is when it was known, and here that is after day 0.

options.text: Yes, if it is lagged by one day
options.why: A one-day lag still leaves it known around day 14, inside the label window.

options.text: Yes, for shares reporting after day 21
options.why: For those the surprise is not known yet either, so it cannot be computed on day 0.

feedback.correct: Known on day 15, used on day 0: target leakage.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare when the surprise is known with day 0.

byKey.yes: Fundamental data leak as easily as prices. Ask when the value was known.

explain.text: The surprise is known only when the report comes out, inside the label window. It also moves the price the label measures, so it would carry a large leak. Use the last surprise reported by day 0 instead.

items.prose: You have 150 rows and 2,000 candidate features, all noise. Each step below is fitted once on all rows, before 5-fold cross-validation.
items.question: Which step inflates the CV score the most?

options.text: Keeping the 20 features most correlated with $y$
Standardising every feature
options.why: A scaler learns from $X$ only; its leak is close to 0. The large leaks read $y$.

options.text: PCA to 10 components
options.why: PCA uses $X$ only. On the seeded data of Lesson 10 its leak rounded to 0.00.

options.text: Taking logs of positive features
options.why: A log has nothing to fit, so it cannot leak at all.

feedback.correct: Selection reads the labels, test labels included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the step that looks at $y$.

byKey.pca: PCA uses $X$ only. The large leaks come from steps fitted on $y$.

explain.text: Choosing 20 of 2,000 by correlation with all labels picks columns that fit every fold's noise. In Lesson 10, 10 of 500 inflated CV $R^2$ by 0.74 on average. Put the selector inside the pipeline.

items.prose: A share database drops delisted firms. Over the period 20% of firms were delisted, and they returned 15 points a year less than the survivors.
items.question: By the survivorship-gap formula, how far does the database overstate the average firm's return?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the share of firms delisted by how much worse they did.

byKey.fifteen: That is the gap between dead and alive firms. Only 20% died, so multiply by 0.20.

explain.text: $P(S^c)\,(E[R \mid S] - E[R \mid S^c]) = 0.20 \times 15 = 3$ points a year. On Lesson 11's panel, 25% deaths gave 5.77 points.

items.prose: A researcher tries 20 independent noise strategies on 4 years of data and keeps the best.
items.question: By the rule of thumb $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$, what Sharpe can the best reach from luck alone?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\sqrt{2 \ln 20}$, then divide by $\sqrt 4 = 2$.

byKey.overT: You divided by 4. The spread of a Sharpe falls with $\sqrt T$, so divide by 2.

explain.text: $\sqrt{2 \ln 20} = 2.448$, and over 4 years that is $2.448/2 = 1.22$. The simulated mean is lower, $1.8675/2 = 0.93$; the rule is a cautious ceiling.

items.prose: A weekly model predicts at the close of day 0 the return over days 1 to 5. By mistake the 5-day momentum feature ends on day 2 instead of day 0.
items.question: How many days of the label does the feature contain?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the days of the feature window after day 0.

byKey.three: You counted day 0. The label starts on day 1.
byKey.five: The window ends on day 2, so only days 1 and 2 overlap.

explain.text: The window covers days −2 to 2; days 1 and 2 are label days. In Lesson 9's noise simulation, 2 days of overlap on a 21-day label already gave 53%.

items.prose: At today's close you predict tomorrow's return. One feature z-scores the share's return over the last 60 days, today's return included, using those 60 days' mean and spread.
items.question: Does it leak?

options.text: No: every input is known at today's close
Yes: it uses today's return
options.why: Today's return is known at today's close, when the prediction is made. Only data after the close leaks.

options.text: Yes: the z-score is fitted on data
options.why: It is fitted, but only on the past 60 days. A fit leaks when it sees rows after the prediction.

options.text: Only if it is cross-sectional
options.why: Across shares or across time, the test is the same: are all inputs known at the close?

feedback.correct: A rolling window that ends at the prediction time is safe.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether each input exists at today's close.

byKey.yes: Today's return is known at today's close, the moment of prediction.

explain.text: All 60 days, today's included, end at the prediction time, so known $\le t$ holds. Had the label been today's return, the same feature would leak.

items.prose: Four ways to pick the universe for a 2010 to 2024 backtest of UK large caps.
items.question: Which is free of look-ahead and survivorship?

options.text: The 100 largest shares as of each rebalance date, dead firms kept
Today's 100 largest shares
options.why: Today's largest are the firms that grew after 2010. That is look-ahead in the choice of firms.

options.text: Shares listed for all of 2010 to 2024
options.why: A full-history filter drops every firm that died, as `dropna(axis=1)` did in Lesson 11.

options.text: The 100 largest of 2010, dropping any that later delisted
options.why: Starting from 2010 is right; dropping later delistings brings survivorship back.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, for each option, whether it uses information from after the rebalance date.

byKey.full: That filter removes every firm that died before 2024.

explain.text: Only the as-of list uses nothing after each date. Keep delisted firms and their delisting returns so the dead count too.

items.prose: A search tried 50 lookbacks of one trend rule, from 100 to 149 days, whose results move almost exactly together. It also tried 5 unrelated signals.
items.question: About how many effective trials is that?

options.text: About 6

options.why: You counted every run. Lookbacks that move together are close to one trial.
The trend rule family is itself at least one trial.
The 5 unrelated signals are separate chances to get lucky.

feedback.correct: One trend family plus five signals: about 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count groups of tries that move together as about one.

byKey.55: You counted raw runs. Nearly identical lookbacks add almost nothing to choose between.

explain.text: Nearly perfectly correlated lookbacks behave as about one try, as in Lesson 12's correlated searches. With 5 unrelated signals, the effective $N$ is about 6; haircut with that, and keep the log of all 55.

items.prose: A team holds out 2023 as a test set. Over six months they score 15 versions of their model on it, fixing something after each look, and report the best.
items.question: What is the 2023 score now?

options.text: The best of 15 tries on 2023, so it carries selection inflation
An honest test score: 2023 was never used for training
options.why: No model was trained on 2023, but 2023 chose among 15 versions. That makes it part of the search.

options.text: A validation score, which is fine to report
options.why: A validation score is fine as a choosing tool. Reported as the final score, it is inflated.

options.text: More reliable, since it was checked 15 times
options.why: Each look was a new try on the same year. More looks mean more inflation.

feedback.correct: A test set used 15 times is a validation set.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what 2023 was used for.

byKey.honest: No training, but 2023 still chose the winner among 15. Selection is a use.

explain.text: Every look that led to a change was a trial on 2023. Lock a fresh period, such as 2024, and score the chosen model on it once.
